analysis.headline: The House passed the Elijah E. Cummings Lower Drug Costs Now Act 230–192 on December 12, 2019, but the Senate read it twice, placed it on its legislative calendar, and never voted on it before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the Department of Health and Human Services to negotiate maximum prices for insulin and for the most expensive brand-name drugs that face no generic competition — starting with at least 25 drugs in 2023 and at least 50 in 2024. Negotiated prices could not exceed 120% of the average price in six other developed countries (or 85% of the U.S. list price if foreign data were unavailable), and they would apply to Medicare and, unless an insurer opted out, to private insurance as well [S2, S3]. It would also require drugmakers to pay rebates when their prices rise faster than inflation, cap seniors' yearly out-of-pocket drug costs and eliminate copays above that cap, add dental, vision, and hearing coverage to Medicare, expand subsidies for low-income beneficiaries, and fund NIH, FDA, and opioid-response programs [S3]. Drugmakers that refused to negotiate would face steep penalties, including an excise tax on sales that starts at 65% and climbs to 95% of the sale price [S3, S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who would get negotiated drug prices, inflation rebates, a lower out-of-pocket cap with no cost-sharing above it, and new dental, vision, and hearing coverage [S3]. Low-income seniors, whose eligibility for premium and cost-sharing subsidies would expand, including automatic qualification for some residents of U.S. territories and some Medicaid beneficiaries [S3]. People with private insurance, who could benefit from the negotiated prices unless their insurer opted out [S2, S3]. Communities served by community health centers and people affected by the opioid epidemic, through new funding streams including an Opioid Epidemic Response Fund [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Current law prohibits HHS from negotiating drug prices under Medicare; the bill would require HHS to negotiate maximum prices for insulin and for at least 25 (2023) then 50 (2024) single-source brand-name drugs with no generic competition, drawn from the drugs with the highest national and Medicare spending [S2, S3].

Negotiated prices could not exceed 120% of the average price in Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Japan, and the United Kingdom, or 85% of the U.S. average manufacturer price where foreign data are unavailable [S2, S3].
Drugmakers would owe rebates to Medicare for covered drugs costing $100 or more whose average manufacturer price rises faster than inflation [S3].

The bill would lower and cap Medicare Part D beneficiaries' annual out-of-pocket spending and eliminate their cost-sharing above that threshold, and let some enrollees spread cost-sharing payments over time [S3].
Medicare would add coverage for dental and oral health services including dentures, hearing aids and hearing treatment, and eyeglasses, contacts, and vision care [S3].

The negotiated maximum prices could also be offered through private group and individual health insurance unless the insurer affirmatively opts out, and nonparticipating insurers would have to publicly disclose that choice [S3, S4].

Compliance would be enforced with civil monetary penalties (ten times the gap between the charged price and the negotiated price), tax penalties, and an excise tax of 65%–95% of sale price during periods of noncompliance [S2, S3, S4].

The bill would fund NIH and FDA innovation projects, create an Opioid Epidemic Response Fund, fund community health centers through FY2025, and prohibit abusive 'spread pricing' by pharmacy benefit managers in Medicaid [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear the direct cost: a new excise tax of 65% of sale price in the first 90 days of noncompliance, rising to 95% after 270 days, which they could not deduct from taxes [S4]; civil monetary penalties of ten times the difference between their price and the negotiated maximum price, up to $1 million per violation of agreement terms [S4]; inflation rebates on Medicare drugs [S3]; and, for drugs without foreign price data, mandatory payments to the Treasury when international price data later show their U.S. price exceeded twice the international benchmark [S4]. Pharmacy benefit managers would also lose the Medicaid 'spread pricing' practice the bill prohibits [S3]. HHS would lose the discretion it has today, since the bill repeals the current-law prohibition on Medicare price negotiation [S2].

drawbacks.text: Opponents' chief stated concern was the effect on new drug development: the House Republican motion to recommit sought to delay the bill's effective date until HHS certified that implementation was not projected to result in fewer new drug applications for unmet medical needs and life-saving cures; it failed 196–226 [S6, S7].

The bill caps prices by reference to what six other countries pay — an approach that shifts the benchmark for U.S. prices to systems where governments restrict drug spending, which is the mechanism through which manufacturers would lose revenue [S2, S4].

The bill limits judicial review: HHS's selection of drugs, its determination of which drugs are eligible, and its determination of the maximum fair price could not be challenged in court, leaving manufacturers no legal avenue to contest pricing decisions [S4].

The benefit to privately insured Americans is qualified: negotiated prices reach private coverage only if the insurer does not opt out, so the guarantee for that population is weaker than for Medicare beneficiaries [S3, S4].

The bill was passed on near-pure party lines — 228 of 230 yes votes were Democrats and only 2 Republicans supported it — signaling that its design had little cross-party buy-in, which matters because the bill could only become law with broader agreement [S8].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers the upside was large and concrete: negotiated prices for the most expensive drugs, inflation rebates, a hard cap on seniors' out-of-pocket drug costs, and new Medicare dental, vision, and hearing benefits [S3]. The costs fall on a concentrated, well-resourced industry — with penalties severe enough (up to a 95% excise tax on sales) that they function less as a tax than as compulsion to negotiate [S4]. The strongest honest objection is the innovation question: opponents argued that capping prices at international benchmarks could mean fewer new drug applications for unmet needs, and the bill answers that concern only by limiting courts' ability to review HHS's pricing decisions [S4, S7] — which addresses the objection by foreclosing challenge rather than by evidence. On balance, the direct benefit to tens of millions of Medicare beneficiaries and privately insured patients was substantial and immediate, while the innovation risk was a credible but unproven projection; the bill's fatal weakness was political, not substantive — it passed the House but the Senate never considered it.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 230–192 on December 12, 2019, but after being received in the Senate and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders in September 2020, it was never brought to a Senate vote before the 116th Congress expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. introduced H.R. 3 on September 19, 2019; it was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor Committees [S1, S2, S5, S6].

The Energy and Commerce Committee held markup sessions in October 2019 and ordered the bill reported (amended) by votes of 24–17 to 30–22; all three committees reported it by December 9, 2019, and it was placed on the Union Calendar [S6].

The House debated the bill on December 11–12, 2019 under a rule (H. Res. 758) allowing four hours of general debate and consideration of amendments; a Republican amendment by Rep. Walden failed, and several Democratic amendments were adopted [S6].

Rep. Upton's motion to recommit with instructions — to delay the bill until HHS certified it would not reduce new drug applications — failed 196–226, with 193 of 196 yes votes from Republicans [S6, S7].
The House passed the bill 230–192 on December 12, 2019: 228 Democrats and 2 Republicans voted yes, while 191 Republicans, 1 Independent, and no Democrats voted no [S8].

The Senate received the bill on December 16, 2019, read it the first time on August 13, 2020, read it the second time and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 521) on September 8, 2020, and no further action was taken [S6, S4].
No Senate vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1].

key_actors.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
key_actors.role: Sponsor; Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee (committee of primary jurisdiction that reported the bill)
key_actors.what_they_did: Introduced H.R. 3 on September 19, 2019 and steered it through Energy and Commerce markup, where it was ordered reported (amended) 24–17 on October 22, 2019 and formally reported December 6, 2019 [S1, S5, S6].

key_actors.name: U.S. Senate
key_actors.role: Chamber that received the bill after House passage and never voted on it
key_actors.what_they_did: Received the bill December 16, 2019; took no action for eight months, then read it the first time (August 13, 2020) and the second time, placing it on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 521) on September 8, 2020 — after which no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended [S6, S4].

key_actors.name: House Democratic Caucus
key_actors.role: Majority party that passed the bill
key_actors.what_they_did: Voted 228–0 in favor of final passage on December 12, 2019 [S8].

key_actors.name: House Republicans
key_actors.role: Minority party that opposed the bill
key_actors.what_they_did: Voted 191–2 against final passage; Rep. Walden offered a failed amendment and Rep. Upton's motion to recommit (to delay the bill until HHS certified no reduction in new drug applications) failed 196–226 [S6, S7, S8].
